adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:141 — Emitting the new task keyword immediately makes new producers incompatible with old workers during a rolling deploy, delaying or dropping outbound assignment syncs.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async is called with a new keyword argument 'assignment_source_dict' (lines 137-143 in sync.py). The task function sync_assignee_outbound in sync_assignee_outbound.py is also modified to accept this new parameter. During a rolling deploy, if a new producer sends a task with 'assignment_source_dict' to an old worker that doesn't have this parameter defined, the task could fail or behave unexpectedly. However, looking more carefully at the task definition, the new parameter has a default value (assignment_source_dict: dict[str, Any] | None = None), which means old workers without this parameter would actually fail with an unexpected keyword argument error. This is a valid deployment compatibility concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:28 — Serializing with asdict exposes the whole dataclass as an unversioned Celery wire contract, so routine field additions can silently invalidate queued provenance

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real architectural concern in the diff. The AssignmentSource dataclass is serialized via asdict() at line 28 and passed through Celery task kwargs (sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async with assignment_source_dict). The from_dict() method at line 31-35 uses cls(**input_dict) which will fail if fields are added/removed between when a task is queued and when it's processed. This is a legitimate versioning concern for async task contracts, though the current implementation does handle errors by returning None. The finding is specific to code in the diff and represents a real design consideration for production systems.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/models/groupassignee.py:15 — A widely imported core model now takes a runtime dependency on an integrations-layer DTO solely for optional provenance, creating a reverse layer dependency

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that src/sentry/models/groupassignee.py (a core model in sentry.models) now imports AssignmentSource from sentry.integrations.services.assignment_source (line 15 in the diff). This creates a dependency from the core models layer to the integrations layer, which is a legitimate architectural concern. The import is used to add an optional parameter to assign() and deassign() methods. While this is a valid design concern about layer dependencies, it's not a bug - the code will function correctly. This is a scope/architecture concern that a reasonable reviewer might raise.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:390 — Embedding assignment-origin suppression in generic should_sync couples every sync type to assignee semantics and can silently disable unrelated synchronization

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that embedding assignment-origin suppression in should_sync couples every sync type to assignee semantics. However, looking at the diff, the sync_source parameter is optional (defaults to None), and the check only activates when sync_source is explicitly provided. The code shows that sync_source is only passed for assignee-related operations (sync_group_assignee_outbound), not for status sync. The status sync path (sync_status_outbound) has a separate assignment_source parameter but the should_sync call for status would not pass this parameter based on the existing code patterns. The design actually allows selective use of the suppression logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:416 — The status-sync interface now carries an unused AssignmentSource parameter, needlessly coupling unrelated provider implementations to assignment provenance

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the abstract method sync_status_outbound now has an assignment_source parameter added (lines 408-417), but this parameter is named 'assignment_source' and relates to status sync, not assignee sync. Looking at the diff, this parameter is added to the abstract method signature but there's no implementation shown that uses it. The concern about coupling status sync to assignment provenance is valid - the parameter name 'assignment_source' suggests it's for tracking where an assignment came from, but it's being added to a status sync method. This is a legitimate architectural concern about the interface design, though the severity is debatable since it's an optional parameter with None default.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — queued is evaluated once at module import, so every later assignment source from that process records a stale timestamp instead of its actual queue time.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default value in the dataclass definition at line 18. In Python, default values are evaluated once at class definition time, not at instance creation time. This means every `AssignmentSource` instance created without explicitly passing a `queued` argument will have the same timestamp from when the module was first imported, rather than the actual time the instance was created. This is a well-known Python gotcha with mutable/callable defaults.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:221 — The lone matching-source test has no second linked integration, so it passes even if a source suppresses all outbound propagation instead of only the originating system.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap. Looking at the test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` (lines 167-227), it only creates one integration and tests that outbound sync is blocked when the assignment source matches that integration. However, the intended behavior (per the comment in mixins/issues.py lines 387-389: 'This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward') is that OTHER integrations should still sync. The test doesn't verify this - it would pass even if the code incorrectly blocked ALL outbound syncs rather than just the originating one. A more complete test would have two integrations and verify the non-matching one still receives the sync call.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:274 — The updated unassign test only covers assignment_source=None, leaving matching-source inbound unassignment cycle prevention unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a gap in test coverage. Looking at the diff, the test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` (lines 161-218) tests that outbound sync is prevented when assignment_source matches the integration during assign operations. However, the `test_assignee_sync_outbound_unassign` test (lines 271-274) only tests with `assignment_source=None`. The deassign method also accepts `assignment_source` parameter (line 207 in groupassignee.py) and passes it to `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (lines 235-237), so there should be a corresponding test for deassign with a matching source integration to verify the cycle prevention works for unassignment as well.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:36 — The queued assertion only checks non-nullness, so it misses that the default is evaluated once and every AssignmentSource receives the same import-time timestamp.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real bug. In the diff at line 17 of assignment_source.py, the default value `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time, not at instance creation time. This is a well-known Python gotcha with mutable/callable defaults. The test at line 36 only checks `assert result.get("queued") is not None`, which would pass even though all instances share the same timestamp. This is a genuine defect in the code.
